section_summary: This section records complaints and British concern about Japanese export prices, especially the October 1949 abolition of most export floor prices. It includes diplomatic reports, parliamentary exchanges, and the Japanese and SCAP memoranda setting out proposed safeguards and the final policy. A separate airgram reports the relaxation of Japanese potato price and distribution controls.

subfiles.title: Complaint about Japanese enamelware export prices
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP’s response to a European association’s complaint that Japanese enamelware was offered at excessively low export prices.
subfiles.summary: SCAP argued that quality and freight costs made factory prices misleading; buyers were instead complaining that landed Japanese prices were too high.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of comments on enamelware prices
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of SCAP’s comments on the enamelware complaint.
subfiles.summary: Jobsis thanks Gay and says he will inform his government.

subfiles.title: Elimination of price controls for Japanese exports
subfiles.from: Arthur R. Ringwalt, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Reports British press and parliamentary reactions to the abolition of Japanese export floor prices.
subfiles.summary: British commentary feared renewed Japanese price cutting, subsidies, and harm to textile producers. The Board of Trade said Britain had been informed before the decision but its assent was neither sought nor required.

subfiles.title: House of Commons exchange on SCAP authority over export prices
subfiles.about: Transmits a parliamentary exchange about SCAP’s authority to abolish Japanese export price controls.
subfiles.summary: The British minister maintained that SCAP could act where the Far Eastern Commission had issued no directive. Members pressed him on consultation and possible effects on British textiles.

subfiles.title: Transmission of British and SCAP memoranda on floor prices
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the United Kingdom Liaison Mission’s concerns and General Marquat’s reply about abolished floor prices.
subfiles.summary: The covering despatch outlines British requests for public safeguards and Marquat’s assurance that unfair methods would be addressed.

subfiles.title: British request for assurances on Japanese export pricing
subfiles.about: Requests a fuller SCAP statement and public assurances against low or repeatedly reduced Japanese export quotations.
subfiles.summary: Lingeman cites British political and industry concern, welcomes the announced pricing principles, and asks SCAP to forbid practices that could disrupt markets. He also suggests a Japanese prime ministerial statement.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply on the elimination of floor prices
subfiles.to: Head of the United Kingdom Liaison Mission in Japan
subfiles.about: Responds to British concerns about unfair Japanese export pricing.
subfiles.summary: Marquat promises efforts against unfair methods and invites specific evidence and proposed remedies.

subfiles.title: House of Commons exchange on the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Transmits questions about why Britain did not raise Japanese export price controls in the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: A British minister said the government expected insufficient support for Commission action; members challenged that decision and questioned the trade consequences.

subfiles.title: Relaxation of Japanese potato controls
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP authorization to relax potato distribution and price controls.
subfiles.summary: Farmers could sell potatoes beyond their quotas on the open market.

subfiles.title: Documents involved in the abolition of Japanese floor prices
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the Japanese plan and SCAP decision governing abolition of export floor prices.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains proposed licensing checks, domestic price comparisons, and safeguards against dumping. SCAP accepted the general plan but rejected industry self-restraint and most proposed commodity exceptions, retaining floor prices temporarily for silk.

subfiles.title: Plan to safeguard exports after abolition of floor prices
subfiles.from: Ministry of International Trade and Industry
subfiles.to: Foreign Trade and Commerce Division, SCAP
subfiles.about: Proposes measures against capital flight, dumping allegations, and foreign retaliation after floor prices end.
subfiles.summary: MITI proposes export license and cargo checks, better overseas price information, contact with buying countries, and industry self-restraint. It warns of limited information and staff and asks to retain floor prices temporarily for selected goods.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to MITI export license offices and proposed exception list
subfiles.from: Ministry of International Trade and Industry
subfiles.to: MITI offices authorized to approve export licenses
subfiles.about: Sets out proposed export price checks and lists commodities that would retain floor prices.
subfiles.summary: The draft directs offices to compare quotations with current and domestic prices, refer suspect applications to MITI, and retain controls on silk and several manufactured goods.

subfiles.title: SCAP decision on MITI’s floor price plan
subfiles.from: F. E. Pichelle, for the Chief, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.to: Ministry of International Trade and Industry
subfiles.about: Approves abolition of export floor prices subject to pricing safeguards and a temporary silk exception.
subfiles.summary: SCAP requires domestic price or production cost benchmarks and exporter guidance on foreign unfair competition rules. It rejects MITI’s wider exception list and directs abolition on October 26, with silk temporarily exempt.
